## Guide to this document

This manuscript brings together the full analysis of *H. longicornis* in Australia, which was developed
in stages in separate folders:

| Stage | Folder (Australia-only version) | Earlier Australia + New Zealand version | Content |
|---|---|---|---|
| Current climate | `code_6/` | `code_3/` (+ `code_3/optimisation/`) | Bias-corrected, transfer-validated consensus MaxEnt model; current suitability; niche comparison |
| Future climate | `code_7/` | `code_4/` | CMIP6 projections, attribution, extrapolation, uncertainty partitioning; re-evaluation of `code_2/` |
| Management extensions | `code_8/` | `code_5/` | Livestock exposure, introduction risk, process model, refugia, warming levels, surveillance |
| Superseded | `code/`, `code_2/` | | First (v1) and second (v2) model iterations, evaluated in Supplementary Methods S1 and S5 |

The Australia-only versions (`code_6`–`code_8`) are the analyses reported here. Their model calibration is
identical to the earlier Australia + New Zealand versions; only the projection domain and the
outputs that depend on it differ (Supplementary Methods S2). This document does not refit any model: every number, table and figure is read from
the saved outputs of those analyses (`outputs_6–8/`, `processed_data_6–8/`, `figures_6–8/`, and
`outputs_2–5/` for comparisons). It therefore renders in a few minutes. Three figures are new
(workflow, synthesis of change, and model development; saved to `figures_9/`).

Figures and tables proposed for the **main text** are boxed in
<span style="color:#1b7837;font-weight:700">green</span>; **supplementary** figures and tables are boxed
in <span style="color:#666;font-weight:700">grey</span> and numbered S1, S2, …. All code is embedded
(**Show code**).
:::

```{r}
# ---- Consensus prediction from the stored MaxEnt lambdas (as in code_7; identical to maxent.jar)
mx_cloglog <- function(L, x) {
  s <- numeric(nrow(x))
  for (j in seq_len(nrow(L$f))) {
    ft <- L$f$feature[j]; lo <- L$f$min[j]; hi <- L$f$max[j]
    val <- if (startsWith(ft, "'")) { v <- x[[substring(ft, 2)]]; ifelse(v <= lo, 0, (v - lo) / (hi - lo)) }
      else if (startsWith(ft, "`")) { v <- x[[substring(ft, 2)]]; ifelse(v >= hi, 0, (hi - v) / (hi - lo)) }
      else if (grepl("\\^2$", ft)) (x[[sub("\\^2$", "", ft)]]^2 - lo) / (hi - lo)
      else if (grepl("\\*", ft)) { p <- strsplit(ft, "\\*")[[1]]; (x[[p[1]]] * x[[p[2]]] - lo) / (hi - lo) }
      else (x[[ft]] - lo) / (hi - lo)
    s <- s + L$f$lambda[j] * pmin(pmax(val, 0), 1)
  }
  1 - exp(-exp(L$H) * exp(s - L$lpn) / L$dn)
}
p_occ <- rowMeans(sapply(lam$final, mx_cloglog, x = occ))
```

# Abstract {.unnumbered}

::: {.abstract-box}
**Aim.** The Asian longhorned tick, *Haemaphysalis longicornis*, has been established in eastern
Australia for more than a century. It transmits *Theileria orientalis* to cattle and is a vector of
several zoonotic pathogens in its native range. We set out to estimate where climate permits the tick to persist in Australia
now and later this century, which climatic factors set those limits, and what the projections imply for
livestock exposure, introduction risk and surveillance.

**Location.** Calibration across the native range (East Asia) and invaded ranges (North America,
Australia, New Zealand and the south-west Pacific); projection to continental Australia and Tasmania.

**Taxon.** *Haemaphysalis longicornis* Neumann (Acari: Ixodidae), parthenogenetic lineage.

**Methods.** We modelled `r kr6$n_occ` thinned, regionally stratified records with MaxEnt, using a
region-balanced target-group background and selecting among ten *a priori* predictor sets by
leave-one-region-out (LORO) and spatial-block cross-validation. The three best configurations formed a
consensus model. It was projected to ten CMIP6 global climate models (GCMs), screened for climate
sensitivity and independence, under four emissions scenarios (SSPs) and four periods to 2100. Future aridity was derived from each GCM's monthly
climate. We quantified range change, its climatic drivers, extrapolation, and the partitioning of
uncertainty among scenario, GCM and model parameters. We then translated suitability into cattle and
human exposure, gravity-model establishment risk, microclimatic refugia, outcomes at global warming
levels and an optimised surveillance design. We also built an independent process-based model of
life-cycle feasibility from published thermal and moisture thresholds.

**Results.** Only predictor sets that included annual mean temperature transferred between
continents. The set chosen by automated collinearity screening, which lacked any absolute
temperature variable, omitted `r pct(cvA("Oceania"))`% of Oceanian records when Oceania was withheld.
The consensus transferred well (mean LORO AUC = `r fmt(cvs$loro_auc)`). Trained without any Oceanian
records, it still ranked Australian localities highly (AUC = `r fmt(aus_eval$auc)`), but invaded-range
records were needed to calibrate suitability levels. Suitable climate currently covers
`r fmt_int(tot[["suitable"]] / 1000)` × 10³ km² (`r fmt(100 * tot[["suitable"]] / land, 1)`% of the land
area): the eastern seaboard from south-east Queensland to Victoria, almost all of Tasmania, and small
areas of South Australia and Western Australia. `r pct(tot[["gap"]] / tot[["suitable"]])`% of it lies more
than 100 km from any known record. The Oceanian niche was equivalent to the native niche. Suitable area
declines by `r mns(-es("245", "2021-2040")$pct_change_med)`% by 2021–2040 and by
`r mns(-es("126", "2081-2100")$pct_change_med)`–`r mns(-es("585", "2081-2100")$pct_change_med)`% by 2081–2100
(SSP1-2.6 to SSP5-8.5). The losses are driven by warming, lie within analogue climates, and are concentrated
at the warm and dry margins. Gains are negligible. Expressed against global warming, the loss is
`r mns(-gs(1.5)$med)`% at 1.5 °C, `r mns(-gs(2)$med)`% at 2 °C and `r mns(-gs(3)$med)`% at 3 °C. Cattle in
suitable climate (`r mil(ex_cur("Cattle"))` million today) decline faster than area. The process model
reproduced the Australian distribution (AUC = `r fmt(filter(kr8$pm_auc, grepl("^Australia", region))$auc_P)`)
but projected smaller losses than the correlative model, and it projected a questing season
`r fmt(ps("245_2041-2060")$dMa_core, 1)`–`r fmt(ps("370_2081-2100")$dMa_core, 1)` months longer in the
persistent core. Establishment risk is concentrated in western Victoria and on the New England
Tablelands, and allocating surveillance by risk detected hidden populations far more efficiently than
uniform or herd-proportional allocation.

**Main conclusions.** The climatic niche of *H. longicornis* has been conserved during invasion,
so a model calibrated across all ranges predicts its Australian distribution well, provided it
includes an absolute temperature gradient and corrects for regional sampling imbalance. Climate change will contract
the Australian range towards a persistent core in south-eastern New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania,
where the tick and theileriosis will remain long-term problems. New incursions will depend on cattle
movement into suitable, uninfested districts rather than on climatic expansion.
:::

**Keywords:** *Haemaphysalis longicornis*; Asian longhorned tick; *Theileria orientalis*; species
distribution model; MaxEnt; model transferability; niche conservatism; climate change; CMIP6;
uncertainty partitioning; biosecurity; surveillance design; Australia


# Introduction

The Asian longhorned tick, *Haemaphysalis longicornis* Neumann, is a three-host ixodid tick native to
temperate East Asia: eastern China, the Korean Peninsula, Japan and the Russian Far East
[@hoogstraal1968; @zhao2020]. It parasitises a wide range of mammals and birds. In Australia it is the
principal vector of *Theileria orientalis*, including the Ikeda genotype responsible for outbreaks of
oriental theileriosis in cattle since 2006 [@kamau2011], and it causes direct production losses
through blood feeding. In East Asia it transmits severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus and
many other pathogens of human and animal health importance [@yu2011; @zhao2020]. The species has
bisexual and parthenogenetic populations, and because a single parthenogenetic female can found a
population, the parthenogenetic form has spread far beyond the native range [@hoogstraal1968]. It has
been established in eastern Australia, New Zealand and several south-west Pacific islands for more than
a century [@heath2016]. Since its detection in New Jersey in 2017 it has spread rapidly across the
eastern United States [@rainey2018]. Only the parthenogenetic form occurs in Australia.

Like other ixodid ticks, *H. longicornis* spends most of its life off the host. Its distribution is
therefore closely tied to climate: temperature governs development, questing and overwinter survival,
and the atmospheric moisture balance governs survival of non-feeding stages [@needham1991; @ogden2016].
In Australia the tick is confined to the humid south-east, which suggests limits set by heat in the north,
by aridity inland, and by cold in the south and at altitude. Australia has warmed by about 1.5 °C since 1910,
and southern Australia is projected to become drier, particularly in the cool season [@grose2020]. If the
tick is limited at both warm and cool margins, climate change could contract its range in some
places and expand it in others. Where and how fast this happens matters for livestock industries,
for theileriosis control, and for biosecurity agencies deciding where to look for new incursions.

Correlative species distribution models (SDMs) are the main tool for estimating where an invasive
species can establish, and several have been developed for *H. longicornis*, mostly to forecast its
spread in North America [@raghavan2019; @rochlin2019; @namgyal2020]. Using such models in an invaded
region raises well-known problems. Presence-only records reflect sampling effort as much as
occurrence, and uncorrected sampling bias distorts both fitted responses and predicted distributions
[@phillips2009]. A model is only useful for an invaded region if the species–climate relationship it
learns transfers across space. That is not guaranteed if invaded populations have expanded into
climates not used in the native range, or have not yet filled the native niche
[@guisan2014; @petitpierre2012]. Complex models and automated variable selection can produce
response surfaces that interpolate well but extrapolate poorly [@radosavljevic2014; @elith2010;
@owens2013]. Despite this, transferability is rarely tested directly; most SDMs are evaluated with
random or spatial cross-validation within the calibration area [@wenger2012; @roberts2017].

Projecting an SDM into future climates adds further problems. Every predictor must be derivable from
climate-model output consistently with the training data. Derived indices approximated by ad hoc
scaling can move outside their physically possible range without any obvious sign of failure. Several CMIP6 GCMs have equilibrium
climate sensitivities (ECS) above the range assessed as very likely by the IPCC, and ensembles
dominated by these models overstate warming for a given emissions pathway [@forster2021;
@hausfather2022]. Future climates may also lie outside the calibration range, where correlative
predictions are unreliable [@elith2010; @mesgaran2014]. Projections carry uncertainty from the
emissions scenario, the GCM and the SDM itself; the SDM component is often large but rarely reported
[@buisson2010; @thuiller2019]. Finally, maps of suitable climate do not on their own tell managers how
many animals are affected, where the tick is likely to be introduced next, or where to look for it.

*H. longicornis* is a strong test case for addressing these problems. It has been recorded on three
continents in both hemispheres, which allows transfer to be tested by withholding entire regions. Its
Australian distribution is long established and reasonably well documented, which provides a check
on whether a globally calibrated model reproduces a known invaded range. An earlier iteration of this
work produced a model that did not transfer between continents and future projections built on
physically impossible predictor values (Supplementary Methods S1, S5), which shows how easily these
problems arise in practice.

Here we develop a transfer-validated model of the climatic suitability of *H. longicornis*, project it
to continental Australia and Tasmania under current and future climates, and translate the projections
into quantities relevant to management. Our aims were to: (i) correct for strongly uneven sampling
effort among regions and select predictors and model complexity explicitly for transferability;
(ii) map current suitability, its limiting factors and suitable but unrecorded areas; (iii) test
whether the climatic niche has been conserved during invasion; (iv) project suitability to 2100 under
four emissions scenarios and ten screened GCMs, attribute the projected change to temperature and moisture,
assess extrapolation and partition uncertainty; (v) check the correlative projections with an
independent process-based model of the tick's life cycle; and (vi) estimate livestock and human exposure,
introduction and establishment risk, microclimatic refugia and outcomes at global warming levels,
and use these to design surveillance.

# Methods

## Overview

The analysis has three linked parts (@fig-workflow). A consensus MaxEnt model was calibrated on records
from the native and all invaded ranges and selected for its ability to transfer between continents. It
was projected to Australia under current climate and to 160 future GCM × scenario × period
combinations. The projections were then combined with livestock, human population, land-use and
movement data, and with a process-based model, to produce management-oriented outputs. Records from New
Zealand and the Pacific islands were retained for calibration because they describe the climates
tolerated by the same parthenogenetic lineage, but all predictions and summaries refer to continental
Australia and Tasmania. The model was reached through two earlier iterations; their diagnosis
and the comparisons that motivated the final design (background, predictor sets, algorithms) are
described in Supplementary Methods S1.

## Occurrence data

Occurrence records of *H. longicornis* were compiled from the Global Biodiversity Information Facility
(GBIF), the Atlas of Living Australia (ALA), a literature compilation of North American and Pacific
records [@rochlin2019] and a georeferenced dataset of ticks in China [@zhang2019]. Records without
coordinates and duplicate localities were removed. The remainder were thinned to a minimum distance of
10 km, and then stratified so that no region contributed more than 35% of records (random subsampling of
East Asian records only). Each record was assigned to a calibration region: East Asia (native range,
including a single Himalayan record), North America (invaded; eastern USA) or Oceania (invaded;
Australia, New Zealand and Pacific islands) (@supptbl-occ).

## Environmental predictors

Candidate predictors were 15 WorldClim 2.1 bioclimatic variables at 2.5 arc-minutes (about 5 km)
[@fick2017], three ENVIREM moisture variables (annual potential evapotranspiration, Thornthwaite
aridity index and climatic moisture index) [@title2018], and mean annual vapour-pressure deficit (VPD)
from CHELSA v2.1 [@karger2017]. BIO8, BIO9, BIO18 and BIO19 were excluded *a priori* because they
combine temperature and precipitation quarters and produce spatial discontinuities.

## Accessible area and bias-corrected background

The accessible area (*M*) [@barve2011] was the union of 1,000-km buffers around all records, clipped to
land, and was partitioned into the three calibration regions by nearest record. To correct for
sampling bias we used a target-group background [@phillips2009] built from all georeferenced
Ixodidae records on GBIF within *M* plus the Chinese tick survey records of @zhang2019. Because GBIF tick
records are overwhelmingly North American, a single global sampling-effort surface would place almost
all background points in North America. We therefore built the sampling-effort surface separately
within each region (Gaussian kernel, σ = 1°, normalised to a maximum of 1 within each region, floor
0.02). The 10,000 background points were allocated among regions in proportion to land area
(@suppfig-bias). A second, independent set of 10,000 points drawn uniformly across *M* was used only for
evaluation, so that all candidate models were compared against the same reference distribution of
available environments. The earlier iterations of the model used a single, unbalanced
background. Replacing it was the largest single improvement in transferability (Supplementary Methods
S1; @supptbl-bg).

## Predictor sets, calibration and selection for transferability

Collinearity was assessed across *M* rather than at occurrence points [@dormann2013]
(@suppfig-cor). Instead of relying on automated stepwise variance-inflation-factor (VIF) selection,
we defined ten candidate predictor sets *a priori*. Each set had four or five variables spanning the
axes that constrain off-host survival and development of ixodid ticks: thermal regime or thermal
limits, temperature variability, moisture supply and desiccation stress [@needham1991; @heath2016].
All sets had |Spearman's ρ| ≤ 0.75 and VIF < 5 across *M* (@supptbl-sets). Set A reproduced the
stepwise-VIF selection of the earlier model iteration and contained no absolute temperature variable.

Models were fitted with MaxEnt 3.4 [@phillips2006; @phillips2017] through `dismo`, with clamping,
without threshold features and with complementary log-log (cloglog) output. Because the purpose of
the model is prediction in an invaded region, configurations were evaluated primarily on
transferability [@wenger2012; @roberts2017], using (1) leave-one-region-out (LORO) cross-validation,
in which models trained on two regions are tested on the third, and (2) spatial block
cross-validation with 5° × 5° blocks in five folds. Test presences were contrasted with evaluation-background
points from the same withheld region or blocks. We recorded the area under the ROC curve (AUC), the
continuous Boyce index (CBI) [@hirzel2006] and the omission rate at the 10th-percentile training-presence
threshold (OR10; expected 0.10) [@radosavljevic2014]. Selection was sequential and prioritised
omission [@radosavljevic2014; @kass2021]. Configurations had to pass an omission filter
(mean LORO OR10 ≤ 0.30 and mean block OR10 ≤ 0.20). Those that passed were ranked by the sum of
their ranks on AUC and CBI under both schemes. The filter matters because, under transfer, a model can
rank sites correctly within a withheld region (high AUC) while predicting uniformly low suitability
there, and so omit almost all of its records. Each of the ten sets was screened over three feature
classes (LQ, LQH, LQHP) and four regularisation multipliers (β = 1, 2, 4, 8). The three top-ranked
sets were then tuned over a full grid (L, LQ, LQH, LQHP × β = 0.5–8) (@suppfig-tuning).

The top-ranked sets differed by small margins relative to the variation among folds. Rather than
choosing one, we combined the selected configuration of each into an unweighted consensus (mean
cloglog of the three members), so that uncertainty in predictor choice is carried into the
predictions. The consensus was evaluated with the same folds, refitting all members within each fold.
Variable importance was summarised as MaxEnt permutation importance. Marginal response curves were computed with
other predictors at their median across presences. Parameter uncertainty was represented by refitting
the consensus to 30 bootstrap resamples of the presence records, resampled within regions.

## Projection to Australia under current climate

Predictions were restricted to continental Australia and Tasmania: the Australian states and
territories (Natural Earth 1:10 m), including near-shore islands but excluding Lord Howe Island,
Macquarie Island and the external territories. Transfer to this domain was evaluated directly: the
consensus fitted without any Oceanian records (the Oceania LORO fold) was evaluated against Australian
records only, with the evaluation-background points in Australia as reference. Suitability was
classified with the 10th-percentile training-presence threshold [@liu2013]; the threshold maximising
sensitivity plus specificity (MSS) is reported for comparison. Extrapolation was assessed with the
multivariate environmental similarity surface (MESS) and the most dissimilar variable [@elith2010].
The limiting factor in each cell was the predictor whose adjustment to its median at presence records
most increased suitability [@elith2010]. Suitable cells more than 100 km from any known Australian
record (training plus ALA records) were designated *suitable but unrecorded*. All areas were computed
from true, latitude-dependent cell areas.

## Niche comparison

To understand why transfer between regions succeeds or fails, we compared the native niche with each
invaded niche in a common environmental space [@broennimann2012; @dicola2017]. A PCA of the model
predictors was calibrated on the evaluation background of all regions. Occurrence and background
densities were estimated on a 100 × 100 grid of the first two axes. We report Schoener's *D*, niche
equivalency and similarity tests (100 randomisations) [@warren2008] and the indices of stability,
expansion and unfilling in shared climates (intersection 0.1) [@guisan2014].

## Future climate scenarios and predictors

Future monthly minimum and maximum temperature and precipitation were taken from the WorldClim 2.1
CMIP6 downscaled projections at 2.5 arc-minutes [@fick2017; @eyring2016]. These are calibrated against
the same 1970–2000 baseline used to train the model. We used four SSPs (SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0,
SSP5-8.5) [@oneill2016] and four 20-year periods (2021–2040 to 2081–2100). GCMs were selected by three
criteria [@forster2021; @meehl2020; @zelinka2020; @knutti2017]: complete data for all SSP × period
combinations; ECS within the IPCC AR6 very likely range of 2–5 K; and one model per modelling centre and
model family. The two Australian ACCESS models were both retained as the national reference models
[@grose2020]. The resulting ten-GCM core ensemble gives 160 GCM × SSP × period combinations
(@supptbl-gcm).

BIO1, BIO2, BIO12, BIO13, BIO15 and BIO17 were computed from monthly data with the WorldClim
definitions, which reproduces the training layers exactly. The Thornthwaite aridity index
[@thornthwaite1948] was computed as in ENVIREM [@title2018], with monthly PET from the Hargreaves
equation [@hargreaves1985]. Because the published ENVIREM layer used in training rests on an
earlier WorldClim baseline, the future change was applied as an anomaly: future aridity = ENVIREM
aridity + (aridity from future monthly climate − aridity from current WorldClim 2.1 monthly climate),
bounded to 0–100 (Supplementary Methods S3; @suppfig-validation). Projections were computed directly
from the fitted MaxEnt feature weights, which reproduce the Java output to within numerical precision
(Supplementary Methods S4).

## Range change, attribution, extrapolation and uncertainty

For each SSP × period we computed the ensemble-median suitability and, for each cell, the proportion of
GCMs projecting suitable climate. Currently suitable cells were *stable* if at least half the GCMs kept
them suitable and *lost* otherwise. Unsuitable cells were *gained* if at least half the GCMs made them
suitable. Changes were *robust* if at least 80% of GCMs agreed. Area statistics are the median and
range across GCMs of each GCM's own binary projection. We also tracked the proportion of grid cells with
known Australian records that remain suitable, and shifts in the latitude centroid and mean elevation of
suitable climate.

To attribute change, each scenario was re-projected with only the temperature predictors (BIO1, BIO2)
changed, and with only the moisture predictors (BIO12, BIO13, BIO15, BIO17, aridity) changed. For two
focal scenarios (SSP2-4.5 2041–2060, a mid-century moderate pathway; SSP3-7.0 2081–2100, an
end-of-century high pathway) each predictor was changed singly, and the predictor causing the largest
change in each lost or gained cell was mapped as its dominant driver. Extrapolation was assessed with
MESS (univariate novelty) and the ExDet NT2 statistic (novel combinations) [@mesgaran2014], and the
effect of clamping by comparing clamped and unclamped predictions. To partition uncertainty, every
bootstrap replicate was projected to every GCM and SSP (1,200 projections per period). The variance in
projected percentage change was decomposed by ANOVA into scenario, GCM, SDM replicate and interactions
[@dinizfilho2009; @buisson2010]. Sensitivity to the GCM ensemble (a likely-ECS subset of six models;
the five-GCM ensemble of the earlier analysis) and to the threshold (MSS) was assessed. The earlier
future-climate analysis was reviewed in detail and its errors quantified (Supplementary Methods S5;
@supptbl-v2).

## Translating suitability into management outputs

**Management categories.** Cells were classified by current suitability and GCM agreement as
*persistent* (suitable now; ≥ 80% of GCMs suitable in future), *at risk* (20–80%), *likely loss*
(≤ 20%), *emerging, robust* (unsuitable now; ≥ 80%), *emerging, possible* (50–80%) or *unsuitable*.

**Livestock and human exposure.** Cattle and sheep (Gridded Livestock of the World v3, 2010
[@gilbert2018]) and people (Gridded Population of the World v4, 2020 [@ciesin2018]) were summed over
cells classed as suitable by each GCM in each scenario. As an indicative index of economic exposure,
the most recent estimate of the cost of theileriosis to Australian cattle producers, AUD 18.8 million
per year [@shephard2022], was divided by the number of cattle in currently suitable climate and scaled
by the projected number of exposed cattle.

**Introduction pressure and establishment risk.** Long-distance spread within Australia occurs
mainly through movements of infested livestock [@heath2016]. Because animal-level movement records are
not public, introduction pressure on each 0.25° unit was approximated with a gravity model from
infested units (suitable and within 100 km of a known record), with a heavy-tailed distance kernel and a
penalty for crossing Bass Strait. Establishment risk was the product of expected introductions
(pressure × destination cattle) and climatic suitability (Supplementary Methods S7).

**Process-based model.** As an independent check on the correlative projections, we built a model of
life-cycle feasibility from published stage-specific developmental thresholds and thermal constants
[@yano1987; @heath2016; @schappach2020] and from moisture tolerances of questing stages [@heath2016]
(Supplementary Methods S6; @supptbl-procpar). It combines the potential generation rate (degree-days),
the number of months suitable for larval questing (saturation deficit), and heat-stress and dry-stress
months into an index *P*. Cells with *P* ≥ 0.5 were treated as physiologically suitable. Parameters were fixed
from the literature, not fitted to occurrences. Future runs used monthly temperatures from the same ten GCMs.

**Microclimatic refugia.** Within areas projected to lose suitability, we flagged potential topographic
refugia (≥ 10% of 30″ sub-cells remaining suitable after lapse-rate downscaling of temperature),
irrigation (≥ 5% of the cell equipped for irrigation [@siebert2013]) and tree cover (≥ 30% [@zanaga2021]).

**Global warming levels.** Each GCM × SSP × period was assigned its global warming level relative to
1850–1900 from the CMIP6 warming-level crossing table [@hauser2022] (Supplementary Methods S8), and
projections within ±0.25 °C of 1.5, 2, 3 and 4 °C were pooled.

**Surveillance design.** Each suitable, uninfested unit was given a prior probability of
harbouring an undetected population proportional to its establishment risk, scaled so that the expected
number of undetected populations (*N*~0~) was 1, 5 or 20. Visits detect an existing population with
probability *p* = 0.2, 0.3 or 0.5. Visits were allocated to maximise the probability of detecting at
least one population, and the result was compared with allocation proportional to cattle and with uniform allocation
(Supplementary Methods S7).

## Software and reproducibility

Analyses were run in R 4.4 with `terra`, `sf`, `dismo` (MaxEnt 3.4), `predicts`, `ecospat`, `envirem`,
`matrixStats` and the `tidyverse`. Code for each component is embedded in the analysis reports
(`code_6`, `code_7`, `code_8`); this manuscript reads their saved outputs.

# Results

## Model selection and transferability

The final dataset comprised `r kr6$n_occ` records: `r sum(occ$region == "East_Asia")` from East Asia,
`r sum(occ$region == "North_America")` from North America and `r sum(occ$region == "Oceania")` from
Oceania, of which `r aus_eval$n` lie in the Australian projection domain (@fig-occ). Of the
`r nrow(sel6$set_res)` set × configuration combinations screened, `r nrow(sel6$ranked_sets)` passed the
omission filter, all from sets `r paste(sort(unique(sel6$ranked_sets$set)), collapse = ", ")`; every
one of these sets contains a direct temperature variable (@supptbl-sets). The temperature-free set A
had no passing configuration. In its best configuration it ranked sites well within withheld regions
(mean LORO AUC = `r fmt(sel6$a_best$loro_auc)`), but it failed to transfer suitability levels: with Oceania
withheld, `r pct(cvA("Oceania"))`% of Oceanian records fell below the training threshold (East Asia:
`r pct(cvA("East_Asia"))`%).

The three top-ranked sets, `r paste(kr6$sel_sets, collapse = ", ")`, each pair annual mean temperature
(BIO1) with moisture-supply and aridity variables. Their tuned configurations were
`r paste(map_chr(kr6$members, ~ sprintf("set %s (%s; %s, β = %s; %d features)", .x$set, paste(.x$vars, collapse = ", "), .x$fc, .x$rm, kr6$n_feat[[.x$set]])), collapse = "; ")`.
Simple, strongly regularised configurations transferred best (@suppfig-tuning).

The consensus discriminated presences from available environments in every withheld region
(@tbl-perf; @supptbl-folds). Transfer to Oceania from the native and North American records alone was
strong (AUC = `r fmt(fold("Oceania")$auc)`, CBI = `r fmt(fold("Oceania")$cbi)`). Restricted to the
`r aus_eval$n` Australian records, the Oceania-withheld consensus ranked occupied sites well above
available environments (AUC = `r fmt(aus_eval$auc)`) but under-predicted suitability levels:
`r pct(aus_eval$or10)`% of Australian records fell below its training threshold. Australian records
occupy the warmer and drier part of the Oceanian niche (median annual mean temperature
`r fmt(filter(au_nz, country == "Australia")$t, 1)` °C and aridity index
`r fmt(filter(au_nz, country == "Australia")$ai, 0)`, against `r fmt(filter(au_nz, country == "New Zealand")$t, 1)` °C and
`r fmt(filter(au_nz, country == "New Zealand")$ai, 0)` for New Zealand). The omitted records lie mostly at the arid inland
margin, so invaded-range records are needed to calibrate suitability in Australia. Transfer to East Asia was weakest
(AUC = `r fmt(fold("East_Asia")$auc)`; OR10 = `r fmt(fold("East_Asia")$or10)`): models trained only on
invaded ranges under-predict the colder, more continental parts of the native range. Spatial-block
cross-validation gave mean AUC = `r fmt(cvs$blk_auc)`, CBI = `r fmt(cvs$blk_cbi)` and
OR10 = `r fmt(cvs$blk_or10)`. Fitted to all records, the model classified `r fmt(aus_ins$pct_suitable, 0)`%
of Australian records as suitable at the 10th-percentile threshold (cloglog = `r fmt(kr6$thr_p10, 3)`;
@supptbl-thr).

::: {.primary-table}

```{r}
#| tbl-cap: "Evaluation of the consensus MaxEnt model. Cross-validated metrics compare withheld records with evaluation-background points from the same withheld region or blocks. AUC = area under the ROC curve; CBI = continuous Boyce index; OR10 = omission at the 10th-percentile training-presence threshold (expected 0.10). *Australia (Oceania withheld)* uses the consensus fitted without any Oceanian records, evaluated on Australian records against background points in Australia. In-sample rows use the consensus fitted to all records; for these, OR10 is the proportion of records below the final threshold."
perf6 |> kable(digits = 3, col.names = c("Evaluation", "Test data", "n", "AUC", "CBI", "OR10"))
```
:::

Annual mean temperature was the only predictor that was important in all three members (permutation
importance `r fmt(min(bio1_imp), 0)`–`r fmt(max(bio1_imp), 0)`%). The aridity index and mean diurnal
range carried most of the remaining importance, and precipitation amounts were largely redundant once
temperature and aridity were included (@fig-response a). Suitability was unimodal in annual mean
temperature, peaking at about 12–15 °C and falling steeply below about 5 °C and above about 20 °C, and
declined monotonically with aridity and with diurnal temperature range (@fig-response b).

(a) Global view; (b) Australia, New Zealand and the south-west Pacific. Records from New Zealand and the Pacific inform calibration only; all predictions refer to Australia."

Rugs show predictor values at presence records by region."

## Current climatic suitability in Australia

Suitable climate is concentrated on the eastern seaboard from south-east Queensland through coastal New
South Wales to eastern and southern Victoria, and across Tasmania, with smaller areas in south-western
Western Australia and south-eastern South Australia (@fig-suit). In total
`r fmt_int(tot[["suitable"]])` km² (`r fmt(100 * tot[["suitable"]] / land, 1)`% of the land area) is
suitable (@tbl-area). Tasmania (`r fmt(filter(area6, jurisdiction == "Tasmania")$pct_suitable, 0)`%),
the Australian Capital Territory, Victoria (`r fmt(filter(area6, jurisdiction == "Victoria")$pct_suitable, 0)`%)
and New South Wales (`r fmt(filter(area6, jurisdiction == "New South Wales")$pct_suitable, 0)`%) have the
largest suitable proportions, and New South Wales has the largest suitable area
(`r k3(filter(area6, jurisdiction == "New South Wales")$suitable_km2)` × 10³ km²). Only
`r fmt(100 * tot[["novel"]] / land, 1)`% of the land area has climate outside the calibration range,
almost all of it in the tropical north-west where suitability is negligible (@suppfig-mess). Bootstrap
uncertainty is low except along the margins of the suitable area (@suppfig-boot). The global projection
reproduces the native range and the invaded range in the eastern United States (@suppfig-global).

Aridity is the most limiting factor across inland Australia. Diurnal temperature range limits
suitability along the western slopes of the Great Dividing Range, high mean temperature limits it in the
tropical north, and low mean temperature reduces it in Tasmania and the Australian Alps
(@suppfig-limit a). Of the suitable area, `r k3(tot[["gap"]])` × 10³ km²
(`r pct(tot[["gap"]] / tot[["suitable"]])`%) lies more than 100 km from any known record. Most of this
is in Tasmania (`r k3(filter(area6, jurisdiction == "Tasmania")$gap_km2)` × 10³ km²), western and
coastal Victoria (`r k3(filter(area6, jurisdiction == "Victoria")$gap_km2)` × 10³ km²), coastal
Queensland north of the known range and south-eastern South Australia (@suppfig-limit b). Predictions
were almost unchanged with a uniform rather than bias-corrected background (Spearman ρ =
`r fmt(kr6$sens_cor)`; binary agreement `r fmt(100 * kr6$bin_agree, 1)`%; @suppfig-sens).

::: {.primary-figure}
```{r}
#| label: fig-suit
#| fig-cap: "Current climatic suitability for *H. longicornis* in continental Australia and Tasmania. (a) Consensus cloglog suitability with known Australian records (training and ALA records; black points). (b) Binary suitability at the 10th-percentile training-presence threshold; pale colours mark cells with climate outside the calibration range (MESS < 0)."
fig(6, "Fig3_current_suitability.png")
```
:::

## Niche conservatism between native and invaded ranges

In the climatic space of the model predictors, the Oceanian and native niches overlapped moderately
(Schoener's *D* = `r fmt(nich_oc$D)`). Equivalency could not be rejected
(P = `r fmt(nich_oc$p_equivalency)`), and the Oceanian niche was more similar to the native niche than
expected from the climates available in Oceania (P = `r fmt(nich_oc$p_similarity, 3)`; @supptbl-niche).
In shared climates, `r pct(nich_oc$stability)`% of the Oceanian niche coincided with the native niche.
Expansion was limited (`r pct(nich_oc$expansion)`%) and directed towards wet climates with evenly
distributed rainfall, typical of coastal south-eastern Australia, Tasmania and New Zealand
(@fig-niche a). About a third of the native niche (`r pct(nich_oc$unfilling)`%) was unfilled in Oceania.
This part corresponds to drier, strongly seasonal summer-rainfall climates with large diurnal ranges,
characteristic of northern and inland China. The North American niche overlapped little with the native niche (*D* =
`r fmt(nich_na$D)`) and was not equivalent to it (P = `r fmt(nich_na$p_equivalency, 3)`). The reason
was not expansion into novel climates but unfilling (`r pct(nich_na$unfilling)`%): North American
records occupy a small part of the climates available there (@fig-niche b).

::: {.primary-figure}
```{r}
#| label: fig-niche
#| fig-cap: "Niche dynamics of *H. longicornis* in climatic space (first two PCA axes of the model predictors, calibrated on the background of all regions). Blue = stability (climates occupied in both ranges); red = expansion (occupied only in the invaded range); green = unfilling (occupied only in the native range). Contours delimit available climates in the native (green) and invaded (red) ranges (100% and 75%). Arrows show the shift of the niche centroid (solid) and background centroid (dashed). (a) East Asia vs. Oceania; (b) East Asia vs. North America."
fig(6, "Fig4_niche_dynamics.png")
```
:::

## Projected climate change and future suitability

Every GCM projects warming across the current range in every scenario. By 2021–2040, annual mean
temperature is about `r fmt(cl("245", "2021-2040"), 1)` °C above the 1970–2000 baseline in all SSPs.
By 2081–2100 ensemble-median warming is `r fmt(cl("126", "2081-2100"), 1)` °C (SSP1-2.6),
`r fmt(cl("245", "2081-2100"), 1)` °C (SSP2-4.5), `r fmt(cl("370", "2081-2100"), 1)` °C (SSP3-7.0) and
`r fmt(cl("585", "2081-2100"), 1)` °C (SSP5-8.5). Changes in annual precipitation are small and of
inconsistent sign, but the aridity index increases in almost all combinations because evaporative
demand rises with temperature (@suppfig-climate, @suppfig-climmaps).

Projected change is dominated by contraction at the warm and dry margins of the range (@fig-change,
@tbl-change, @suppfig-futsuit). Suitable area changes by `r pcr("245", "2041-2060")` by 2041–2060 under
SSP2-4.5. By 2081–2100 the change is `r pcm("126", "2081-2100")`% under SSP1-2.6,
`r pcm("245", "2081-2100")`% under SSP2-4.5, `r pcr("370", "2081-2100")` under SSP3-7.0 and
`r pcm("585", "2081-2100")`% under SSP5-8.5. Gains are negligible in every scenario
(≤ `r k3(max(filter(ens7, unit == "Australia")$gain_med))` × 10³ km²). Losses are concentrated in coastal
and subcoastal Queensland, the northern rivers and western slopes of New South Wales, inland and western
Victoria, south-eastern South Australia and south-western Western Australia. Queensland and Western
Australia lose most of their suitable area, whereas Tasmania is almost entirely stable (@tbl-area). The suitable area contracts
towards the south-east and to higher ground. By 2081–2100 its centroid moves
`r fmt(abs(shift("245", "lat_centroid")), 1)`° (SSP2-4.5) to `r fmt(abs(shift("585", "lat_centroid")), 1)`°
(SSP5-8.5) poleward, and its mean elevation rises by `r fmt(shift("245", "elev_mean"), 0)`–`r fmt(shift("585", "elev_mean"), 0)` m
(@suppfig-shift). Individual GCMs agree on where losses occur and differ mainly in their extent
(@suppfig-pergcm).

::: {.primary-figure}
```{r}
#| label: fig-change
#| fig-cap: "Projected change in climatically suitable area relative to 1970–2000 for each emissions scenario (columns) in 2041–2060 and 2081–2100 (rows). Stable, loss and gain classes use the majority of ten GCMs; *robust* indicates agreement of at least 80% of GCMs. Ensemble-median suitability maps are in @suppfig-futsuit and @suppfig-otherperiods."
fig(7, "Fig3_range_change.png")
```
:::

::: {.primary-table}
```{r}
#| label: tbl-area
#| tbl-cap: "Climatically suitable area by state and territory. Current values are from the current-climate projection; *unrecorded* is suitable area more than 100 km from any known record. Future columns give the median percentage change across ten GCMs, with the GCM range in brackets (change is computed after coastal cells outside the state polygons are assigned to the nearest jurisdiction, so it refers to a marginally larger area)."
fut_cols <- ens7 |> filter(unit != "Australia", (ssp == "245" & period == "2041-2060") | (ssp %in% c("245", "370") & period == "2081-2100")) |>
  mutate(col = paste(ssp_lab[ssp], gsub("-", "–", period)),
         val = ifelse(is.finite(pct_change_med), sprintf("%s [%s, %s]", sgn(pct_change_med), sgn(pct_change_lo), sgn(pct_change_hi)), "–")) |>
  dplyr::select(unit, col, val) |> pivot_wider(names_from = col, values_from = val)
fut_au <- ens7 |> filter(unit == "Australia", (ssp == "245" & period == "2041-2060") | (ssp %in% c("245", "370") & period == "2081-2100")) |>
  transmute(unit = "Australia (total)", col = paste(ssp_lab[ssp], gsub("-", "–", period)),
            val = sprintf("%s [%s, %s]", sgn(pct_change_med), sgn(pct_change_lo), sgn(pct_change_hi))) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = col, values_from = val)
area6 |> left_join(bind_rows(fut_cols, fut_au), by = c("jurisdiction" = "unit")) |>
  transmute(`State or territory` = jurisdiction, `Land (10³ km²)` = k3(land_km2), `Suitable (10³ km²)` = k3(suitable_km2, 1),
            `Suitable (%)` = fmt(pct_suitable, 1), `Unrecorded (10³ km²)` = k3(gap_km2, 1),
            across(starts_with("SSP"), ~ replace_na(.x, "–"), .names = "Δ {.col} (%)")) |>
  kable(align = "lrrrrrrr")
```
:::

::: {.primary-table}
```{r}
#| label: tbl-change
#| tbl-cap: !expr 'paste0("Projected suitable area, known localities remaining suitable, and exposure of cattle, sheep and people in Australia (median and, in brackets, range across ten GCMs). *Known localities* is the percentage of grid cells with a known Australian record that are suitable. Livestock (GLW3, 2010) and population (GPW v4, 2020) are held constant. *Cost* is the indicative annual cost of theileriosis to cattle producers, scaling AUD 18.8 million per year [@shephard2022] by exposed cattle (AUD ", fmt(kr8$cost_head, 2), " per exposed head).")'
rng <- function(m, l, h, f = identity, d = 0) { f <- rlang::as_function(f); sprintf("%s [%s, %s]", fmt(f(m), d), fmt(f(l), d), fmt(f(h), d)) }
sel_sc <- expand_grid(ssp = ssps, period = c("2041-2060", "2081-2100"))
area_rows <- ens7 |> filter(unit == "Australia") |> semi_join(sel_sc, by = c("ssp", "period")) |>
  transmute(ssp, period, `Suitable (10³ km²)` = rng(suitable_med, suitable_lo, suitable_hi, ~ .x / 1000),
            `Change (%)` = sprintf("%s [%s, %s]", sgn(pct_change_med), sgn(pct_change_lo), sgn(pct_change_hi)),
            `Known localities (%)` = rng(known_suitable_med, known_suitable_lo, known_suitable_hi, ~ 100 * .x))
expo_rows <- expo8 |> filter(unit == "Australia") |> semi_join(sel_sc, by = c("ssp", "period")) |>
  transmute(ssp, period, group, v = rng(med, lo, hi, ~ .x / 1e6, 1)) |> pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = v)
cost_rows <- kr8$cost_proj |> mutate(ssp = names(ssp_lab)[match(as.character(ssp_l), ssp_lab)], period = as.character(period)) |>
  semi_join(sel_sc, by = c("ssp", "period")) |> transmute(ssp, period, Cost = rng(med, lo, hi, ~ .x / 1e6, 1))
cur_row <- tibble(Scenario = "Current (1970–2000)", Period = "", `Suitable (10³ km²)` = k3(tot[["suitable"]]), `Change (%)` = "",
                  `Known localities (%)` = pct(kr7$known_cur), Cattle = mil(ex_cur("Cattle")), Sheep = mil(ex_cur("Sheep")),
                  People = mil(ex_cur("People")), Cost = "18.8")
fut <- area_rows |> left_join(expo_rows, by = c("ssp", "period")) |> left_join(cost_rows, by = c("ssp", "period")) |>
  arrange(period, ssp) |> transmute(Scenario = ssp_lab[ssp], Period = gsub("-", "–", period), `Suitable (10³ km²)`, `Change (%)`,
                                    `Known localities (%)`, Cattle, Sheep, People, Cost)
bind_rows(cur_row, fut) |>
  rename(`Cattle (M)` = Cattle, `Sheep (M)` = Sheep, `People (M)` = People, `Cost (AUD M yr⁻¹)` = Cost) |>
  kable(align = "llrrrrrrr")
```
:::

## Trajectories, warming levels and exposure

Losses accumulate steadily through the century (@fig-trajectory a). Much of the projected contraction
has already occurred by 2021–2040 (`r pcm("245", "2021-2040")`% under SSP2-4.5), when the four
scenarios are still indistinguishable. They diverge after mid-century: under SSP1-2.6 losses stabilise
at about `r mns(-es("126", "2081-2100")$pct_change_med)`%, whereas under SSP3-7.0 and SSP5-8.5 they
continue to the end of the century. Expressed against the global warming level of each projection, the
results collapse onto a single, nearly linear relationship (@fig-trajectory b; @tbl-gwl):
suitable area changes by `r sgn(gs(1.5)$med)`% at 1.5 °C, `r sgn(gs(2)$med)`% at 2 °C,
`r sgn(gs(3)$med)`% at 3 °C and `r sgn(gs(4)$med)`% at 4 °C. In the ten core GCMs the median year of
reaching 2 °C is `r round(filter(kr8$gwl_year, ssp == "245", warming_level == 2)$year_med)` under SSP2-4.5
(@supptbl-gwlyear).

Of the grid cells with known Australian records, `r pct(kr7$known_cur)`% are climatically suitable under
the baseline climate. This falls to `r kn("245", "2041-2060")`% by 2041–2060 under SSP2-4.5 and to
`r kn("585", "2081-2100")`–`r kn("126", "2081-2100")`% by 2081–2100, from SSP5-8.5 to SSP1-2.6 (@fig-trajectory c). The localities
that become unsuitable are mostly in south-east Queensland and northern New South Wales.

`r mil(ex_cur("Cattle"))` million cattle and `r mil(ex_cur("Sheep"))` million sheep are in suitable
climate today. This is a minority of Australia's herd, most of which is in the semi-arid and tropical
north. Livestock exposure falls faster than area, because the areas lost carry more cattle per unit
area than the persistent core. Cattle in suitable climate change by `r sgn(ex("Cattle", "245", "2041-2060")$pct_med)`% by
2041–2060 under SSP2-4.5 and by `r sgn(ex("Cattle", "126", "2081-2100")$pct_med)`% to
`r sgn(ex("Cattle", "585", "2081-2100")$pct_med)`% by 2081–2100, from SSP1-2.6 to SSP5-8.5 (@fig-trajectory d, @tbl-change;
@suppfig-livestock). The indicative cost of theileriosis scales accordingly, from AUD 18.8 million to
AUD `r fmt(cp("245", "2041-2060")$med / 1e6, 1)` million per year by 2041–2060 (SSP2-4.5). The
`r mil(ex_cur("People"))` million people living in suitable climate, who include much of the populations
of Brisbane, Sydney, Melbourne and Hobart, define the population potentially exposed to
*H. longicornis*-borne zoonoses.

```{r}
#| label: synthesis-figure-data
#| code-summary: "Show code: data for the synthesis figure (new)"
traj_base <- function(d, v0) bind_rows(d, tibble(ssp_l = factor(ssp_lab, levels = ssp_lab), year = 1985, med = v0, lo = v0, hi = v0))
tr_area <- ens7 |> filter(unit == "Australia") |>
  transmute(ssp_l = factor(ssp_lab[ssp], levels = ssp_lab), year = per_mid[period], med = pct_change_med, lo = pct_change_lo, hi = pct_change_hi) |>
  traj_base(0)
tr_known <- ens7 |> filter(unit == "Australia") |>
  transmute(ssp_l = factor(ssp_lab[ssp], levels = ssp_lab), year = per_mid[period], med = 100 * known_suitable_med,
            lo = 100 * known_suitable_lo, hi = 100 * known_suitable_hi) |> traj_base(100 * kr7$known_cur)
tr_cattle <- expo8 |> filter(group == "Cattle", unit == "Australia") |>
  transmute(ssp_l = factor(ssp_lab[ssp], levels = ssp_lab), year = per_mid[period], med = pct_med, lo = pct_lo, hi = pct_hi) |> traj_base(0)
gwl_pts <- summ7 |> filter(unit == "Australia", set == "core") |> dplyr::select(id, pct_change) |>
  inner_join(gwl8, by = "id") |> mutate(ssp_l = factor(ssp_lab[ssp], levels = ssp_lab))
```

::: {.primary-figure}
```{r}
#| label: fig-trajectory
#| fig-cap: "Synthesis of projected change in Australia. (a) Change in climatically suitable area through the century relative to 1970–2000 (lines: median across ten GCMs; ribbons: GCM range). (b) The same change for each of the 160 GCM × SSP × period projections against its global warming level (relative to 1850–1900); open symbols mark warming levels estimated from local warming beyond the last tabulated crossing; the line is a LOESS smooth. (c) Percentage of grid cells with known Australian records that remain suitable. (d) Change in the number of cattle in suitable climate."
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 8.5
xb <- scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1985, per_mid), labels = c("1970–\n2000", gsub("-", "–\n", periods)))
traj_plot <- function(d, ylab, tag, h0 = 0) ggplot(d, aes(year, med, colour = ssp_l, fill = ssp_l)) +
  { if (!is.null(h0)) geom_hline(yintercept = h0, colour = "grey60") } +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), alpha = 0.12, colour = NA) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) + geom_point(size = 1.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = ssp_col, name = NULL) + scale_fill_manual(values = ssp_col, name = NULL) + xb +
  labs(x = NULL, y = ylab, tag = tag)
p_a <- traj_plot(tr_area, "Change in suitable area (%)", "a")
p_b <- ggplot(gwl_pts, aes(gwl, pct_change)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = ssp_l, shape = gwl_capped), alpha = 0.75, size = 1.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", span = 0.9, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.8, se = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = ssp_col, guide = "none") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = 16, `TRUE` = 1), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Global warming level (°C above 1850–1900)", y = "Change in suitable area (%)", tag = "b")
p_c <- traj_plot(tr_known, "Known localities suitable (%)", "c", h0 = NULL)
p_d <- traj_plot(tr_cattle, "Change in cattle in suitable climate (%)", "d")
p_syn <- (p_a + p_b) / (p_c + p_d) + plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Drivers, extrapolation and sources of uncertainty

Warming is the main driver of the projected losses (@fig-drivers). Changing only the temperature
predictors reduced suitable area by `r mns(-at("245", "2041-2060", "t"))`% by 2041–2060 under SSP2-4.5
and by `r mns(-at("370", "2081-2100", "t"))`% by 2081–2100 under SSP3-7.0. Changing only the moisture
predictors reduced it by `r mns(-at("245", "2041-2060", "m"))`% and `r mns(-at("370", "2081-2100", "m"))`%,
against combined losses of `r mns(-at("245", "2041-2060", "c"))`% and `r mns(-at("370", "2081-2100", "c"))`%.
Most of the moisture effect comes from the aridity index (@supptbl-drivers), which rises mainly because
warming increases evaporative demand. Under SSP3-7.0 in 2081–2100, warming alone would remove
`r fmt(dl("370_2081-2100", "bio1"), 0)` × 10³ km² of currently suitable climate and increased aridity alone
`r fmt(dl("370_2081-2100", "aridity_idx"), 0)` × 10³ km². Rising temperature dominates losses along the
Queensland and New South Wales coast and ranges; aridity and diurnal range dominate along the southern
margin in Victoria, South Australia and south-western Western Australia (@fig-drivers b, @suppfig-drivervars).

Climates outside the calibration range are extensive but confined to areas that are unsuitable in any
case. Univariate novelty, driven almost entirely by annual mean temperature above the warmest calibration
conditions, covers `r fmt(100 * min(filter(ens7, unit == "Australia")$novel_univariate_med) / land, 0)`–`r fmt(100 * max(filter(ens7, unit == "Australia")$novel_univariate_med) / land, 0)`%
of the land area, all in tropical and arid northern Australia. No novel combinations of individually
analogue values occurred, and `r an <- 100 * min(with(filter(ens7, unit == "Australia"), suitable_analogue_med / suitable_med)); if (an > 99.95) "all" else paste0("at least ", fmt(an, 1), "% of")`
projected suitable area lies in analogue climate in every scenario (@suppfig-novelty, @supptbl-extrap).
Projected range change therefore does not depend on extrapolation or clamping.

The GCM accounts for most of the variance in projected change until mid-century
(`r fmt(vpv("2041-2060", "Climate model (GCM)"), 0)`% in 2041–2060; emissions scenario
`r fmt(vpv("2041-2060", "Emissions scenario (SSP)"), 0)`%). By 2081–2100 the emissions scenario is the
largest source (`r fmt(vpv("2081-2100", "Emissions scenario (SSP)"), 0)`%), followed by the GCM
(`r fmt(vpv("2081-2100", "Climate model (GCM)"), 0)`%). SDM parameter uncertainty contributes
`r fmt(vpv("2081-2100", "SDM parameters (bootstrap)"), 0)`–`r fmt(vpv("2041-2060", "SDM parameters (bootstrap)"), 0)`%
(@suppfig-uncert, @supptbl-vp). GCM uncertainty is spatially concentrated in south-east Queensland
and northern New South Wales, where losses occur. Excluding GCMs with ECS above 4 K changed projected
losses by at most `r fmt(max(abs(filter(kr7$set_cmp, grepl("Likely", ensemble))$med - filter(kr7$set_cmp, grepl("Core", ensemble))$med)), 1)`
percentage points, and the MSS threshold gave similar losses (@supptbl-ensens, @suppfig-ensens).

::: {.primary-figure}
```{r}

#| fig-cap: "Climatic drivers of projected change. (a) Change in suitable area when only the temperature predictors (BIO1, BIO2), only the moisture predictors (BIO12, BIO13, BIO15, BIO17, aridity), or all predictors change to future values (bars: median across GCMs; whiskers: range). (b) Dominant driver in cells projected to be lost or gained (the predictor whose individual change most decreases or increases suitability; ensemble median) for SSP2-4.5 2041–2060 and SSP3-7.0 2081–2100."
fig(7, "Fig5_drivers.png")
```
:::

## An independent process-based check

With all parameters fixed from laboratory and field studies, the process-based index separated
occurrence records from available environments in every region (AUC =
`r fmt(filter(kr8$pm_auc, region == "All")$auc_P)` overall; `r fmt(filter(kr8$pm_auc, region == "Oceania")$auc_P)`
in Oceania and `r fmt(filter(kr8$pm_auc, grepl("^Australia", region))$auc_P)` for Australian records;
@supptbl-procval). It classified `r pct(kr8$pm_agree[["known_ok"]])`% of cells with known Australian
records as suitable and agreed with the SDM in `r pct(kr8$pm_agree[["binary"]])`% of cells (@fig-process a, b).
Its limits had clear mechanistic causes: dry-stress months exclude the inland, and too few larval
questing months and slow development exclude the coldest highlands (@suppfig-proccomp). Without the
dry-stress term it overpredicted strongly (`r fmt_int(filter(kr8$sens_K, is.na(D_max))$area_P05 / 1000)` × 10³ km²).

The two model types disagree about the future. In the process model, physiologically suitable area
changes by `r sgn(100 * (ps("245_2041-2060")$area_P / ps("245_2041-2060")$area_P_cur - 1))`% by 2041–2060
under SSP2-4.5 and `r sgn(100 * (ps("370_2081-2100")$area_P / ps("370_2081-2100")$area_P_cur - 1))`% by
2081–2100 under SSP3-7.0. Only `r pct(ps("245_2041-2060")$sdm_loss_also_proc)`–`r pct(ps("370_2081-2100")$sdm_loss_also_proc)`%
of the area the SDM projects to lose is also lost in the process model, mainly along the inland margin
where dry-stress months increase. In the persistent core, warming lengthens the nymph and adult
questing season by `r fmt(ps("245_2041-2060")$dMa_core, 1)` months by 2041–2060 under SSP2-4.5 and by
`r fmt(ps("370_2081-2100")$dMa_core, 1)` months by 2081–2100 under SSP3-7.0. It also raises the potential
generation rate by `r fmt(ps("245_2041-2060")$dG_core, 2)`–`r fmt(ps("370_2081-2100")$dG_core, 2)` generations
per year, with the largest increases in Tasmania and the Victorian highlands (@fig-process c).

::: {.primary-figure}
```{r}
#| label: fig-process
#| fig-cap: "Process-based model of life-cycle feasibility. (a) Index *P* under current climate. (b) Agreement between the process model (*P* ≥ 0.5) and the SDM. (c) Change in the length of the nymph and adult questing season (months) within the persistent core range (≥ 80% of GCMs suitable) for the two focal scenarios (median across ten GCMs)."
fig(8, "Fig3_process_model.png")
```
:::

## Introduction risk, refugia and surveillance

Under SSP2-4.5 in 2041–2060, `r fmt(mg("245_2041-2060", "Persistent (robust)"), 0)` × 10³ km² of the
current range is persistent, `r fmt(mg("245_2041-2060", "At risk (uncertain)"), 0)` × 10³ km² at risk and
`r fmt(mg("245_2041-2060", "Likely loss"), 0)` × 10³ km² likely to be lost (@fig-mgmt; @supptbl-mgmtarea).
By 2081–2100 under SSP3-7.0 the persistent core shrinks to `r fmt(mg("370_2081-2100", "Persistent (robust)"), 0)` × 10³ km².
It comprises coastal and highland New South Wales south of about 30°S, eastern and southern Victoria
and Tasmania. Robust emerging areas are negligible (`r fmt(mg("245_2041-2060", "Emerging (robust)"), 1)` × 10³ km²
under SSP2-4.5 2041–2060), so climate change does not open substantial new areas to the tick. Within the
area projected to be lost by 2041–2060 under SSP2-4.5, `r pct(kr8$ref_lapse$lapse6.5[1] / kr8$ref_lapse$loss[1])`%
contains topographic refugia. Including irrigation and tree cover,
`r fmt(loss_mg_pct("SSP2-4.5 2041–2060"), 0)`% contains at least one potential refuge type (@suppfig-refugia,
@supptbl-refugia). Areas without any refuge are mostly cleared, unirrigated pasture on the inland and western margin.

`r fmt_int(sum(units8$infested))` of `r fmt_int(nrow(units8))` 0.25° units were classed as infested. Introduction pressure
is highest immediately inland of the infested coastal belt in New South Wales and Victoria and lowest in
Western Australia and, because of the sea crossing, in Tasmania. Combined with climatic suitability,
establishment risk is concentrated in western Victoria (the Western District and Glenelg region) with
the adjacent south-east of South Australia, and in isolated suitable units on the New England
Tablelands and in south-east Queensland (@fig-risk a). Tasmania is suitable throughout but carries only
`r fmt(100 * tas_share, 1)`% of the total establishment risk under the primary sea-crossing penalty. The
ranking was robust to the kernel parameters (ρ ≥ `r fmt(min(kr8$sens_gamma$rho_pressure), 2)`) but less so
to the sea-crossing penalty (@supptbl-gravsens).

Risk-based allocation of surveillance was much more efficient than the alternatives (@fig-risk b). With
five undetected populations and a 30% chance that a visit detects an existing population, 100
risk-allocated visits detect at least one population with probability
`r fmt(sc100("Risk-based (optimal)"), 2)`, compared with `r fmt(sc100("Proportional to cattle"), 2)` for
allocation proportional to cattle and `r fmt(sc100("Uniform"), 2)` for uniform allocation. Uniform allocation
`r if (length(uni_match)) { b <- sort(unique(kr8$surv_curve$budget)); paste0("needs between ", fmt_int(max(b[b < min(uni_match)])), " and ", fmt_int(min(uni_match)), " visits to match this") } else "does not match this even with 1,000 visits"`.
In a reference design of 250 visits, `r sv("Victoria")` go to Victoria, `r sv("New South Wales")` to New
South Wales and `r sv("South Australia")` to South Australia (@supptbl-survjur, @supptbl-survtop). If all
visits are negative, the expected number of undetected populations among candidate units falls from
`r fmt(sum(cand8$pi), 1)` to `r fmt(sum(cand8$post), 1)` (@suppfig-post). Tasmania receives `r if (sv("Tasmania") == 0) "no" else sv("Tasmania")`
visits under the primary model, a result that depends on the assumed difficulty of Bass Strait crossings.

# Discussion

A model selected explicitly for transfer between continents reproduces the Australian distribution
of *H. longicornis* and shows that its range is set by heat in the north, aridity and continental
temperature regimes inland, and cold in Tasmania and the Alps. Under every emissions scenario, climate
change contracts that range from its warm and dry margins towards a persistent core in south-eastern
New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania, and it opens almost no new climatically suitable land. In
practice this means the tick and *T. orientalis* will remain a problem in south-eastern Australia for
the foreseeable future, while future incursions will depend on livestock movement into districts that
are already suitable rather than on climatic expansion. We discuss the methodological lessons first and
then the implications for management (@tbl-mgmt).

## Transferability depends on absolute temperature and on regional sampling design

Two choices largely determined whether the model transferred. The first was the treatment of sampling
bias. Because GBIF tick records are dominated by North American data, a single global sampling-effort
surface contrasts East Asian and Oceanian presences against very few local background points. In our
first two model iterations this alone reduced mean LORO AUC to about 0.5 (@supptbl-bg). Normalising
sampling effort within regions and allocating background by area corrects for survey intensity within
regions without letting differences in data volume among countries dominate the fitted niche. Once
the regions were balanced, predictions hardly depended on whether the background was bias-corrected or
uniform.

The second choice was the predictor set. Stepwise VIF selection removed every absolute temperature
variable because temperature is collinear with VPD, PET and the thermal extremes. The resulting model
discriminated well within withheld regions but omitted every Oceanian record when Oceania was withheld.
Correlated variables such as VPD and isothermality can stand in for temperature within a calibration
region, but the relationships among them differ between continents, so only a direct thermal gradient
constrains predictions consistently. This is biologically expected: development, questing and
overwinter survival of ixodid ticks are governed by temperature, and off-host survival by the
atmospheric moisture balance [@needham1991; @heath2016]. Our results add to evidence that predictors
chosen on ecological grounds and evaluated by transfer give more reliable models for invasive species
than collinearity screening and within-region cross-validation [@wenger2012; @dormann2013; @valavi2022].
They also show that AUC alone is a poor guide under transfer. An omission filter caught failures that
discrimination metrics missed, and among algorithms MaxEnt had the lowest transfer omission and the
best calibration (@supptbl-alg).

## Niche conservatism and the value of invaded-range records

The Oceanian niche was equivalent to and more similar than expected to the native niche, with high
stability and limited expansion. This is consistent with the general pattern of niche conservatism
during invasion [@petitpierre2012; @guisan2014] and explains why native-range information transfers
well to Australia. The unfilled part of the native niche consists of drier, strongly seasonal
summer-rainfall climates. In Australia comparable rainfall regimes occur mainly in the monsoonal north,
where temperatures exceed the species' optimum, so unfilling probably reflects how climatic axes combine
in Oceania rather than an inability of the lineage to tolerate those conditions. The very low overlap
with North America has a different cause: records there cover a small subset of available climates, the
expected signature of a population still spreading after its detection in 2017 [@rainey2018]. Models
calibrated only on North American records would greatly underestimate the species' tolerance. Even so,
native-range information alone was not enough. Trained without Oceanian records, the consensus ranked
Australian sites well but under-predicted their suitability, particularly at the arid inland margin.
New Zealand records, although outside the projection domain, document persistence of the same lineage
in cool, wet maritime climates comparable to those of Tasmania and southern Victoria, which are poorly
represented among Australian records. Pooling all three ranges is therefore preferable to calibrating on
native or invaded records alone.

## A contracting range anchored in the south-east

The contraction follows directly from the fitted niche. Suitability is unimodal in annual mean
temperature with an optimum of about 12–15 °C, and much of the northern part of the current range in
south-east Queensland and northern New South Wales already lies on the warm side of it. Warming of
1–4 °C pushes these areas beyond the edge of suitable climate, while increasing evaporative demand
erodes the southern and inland margins. Tasmania and the Victorian highlands lie in the cool, humid part of
the niche, so warming moves them towards the optimum rather than away from it. The losses are not an artefact of extrapolation:
they occur within analogue climates, which include the native range in southern China and the
south-eastern United States, both warmer than coastal Queensland. Because the model was trained on
1970–2000 climate, part of the projected contraction, about a tenth of the range by 2021–2040, has
probably already happened. Historical records from the northern margin may therefore describe
populations that are now climatically marginal. This offers a direct test of the projections: declining
tick abundance or *T. orientalis* prevalence at the northern margin since the 1990s would support them.

For decisions over the next few decades, the main uncertainty is which GCM best represents regional
climate, not which emissions pathway is followed. Weighting GCMs by their skill over eastern
Australia, or using regionally downscaled projections, would narrow near-term projections more than
refining the SDM [@knutti2017; @grose2020]. For the end of the century, projections are better framed as
conditional on emissions or on warming level. Expressed against global warming, outcomes fall on a
single curve (roughly a sixth of the suitable area lost at 2 °C and a quarter at 3 °C), which links
them directly to national climate-risk frameworks [@hausfather2022].

## Correlative and mechanistic projections disagree at the warm margin

The process-based model was built from laboratory thresholds and field tolerances, not from occurrence
records, so it provides an independent test of the correlative model [@kearney2009]. That it reproduces the known Australian distribution almost as well as the SDM indicates that
the correlative model has captured real physiological limits: dry-season desiccation inland, cold in the
south and at altitude, and an annual life cycle across the core. The two models disagree about the
warm margin. The SDM has learned from the native and invaded ranges that suitability declines above
about 15–20 °C mean annual temperature, whereas the process model has no thermal penalty below its
heat-stress threshold, so in it warming simply accelerates development. Either the SDM's warm-side
decline reflects processes absent from the process model (warm-season mortality of eggs and unfed
larvae, disruption of the diapause that synchronises the life cycle, competition with other ticks or
changes in hosts), or it partly reflects limited sampling of hot climates. Field monitoring of tick
abundance along the northern margin is the most direct way to tell these explanations apart. Until
then, SDM losses at the warm margin should be treated as an upper bound and the process-model losses
as a lower bound. The process model's projections of seasonality are more robust. A questing season one
to two and a half months longer in the core range, and more potential generations per year, affect the
timing and frequency of acaricide treatment and the period over which calves are exposed to
*T. orientalis*.

## Lessons from the earlier projections

An earlier iteration of this analysis reported contractions of a similar magnitude, but for largely
artefactual reasons (Supplementary Methods S5; @supptbl-v2). It projected a model that did not
transfer between continents (LORO AUC `r fmt(min(v2_loro$auc))`–`r fmt(max(v2_loro$auc))`), and it derived
future aridity by scaling with ratios of Celsius temperatures. The resulting aridity exceeded its theoretical maximum across
`r fmt(min(kr7$v2_ai_stats$pct_above_100), 0)`–`r fmt(max(kr7$v2_ai_stats$pct_above_100), 0)`% of Australian land,
which accounts for most of the extrapolation reported. Its GCM ensemble was weighted towards
high-sensitivity models, and its single-latitude cell-area approximation inflated areas. The agreement
between its numbers and ours is therefore coincidental. The general lesson is that projections are
only as reliable as the weakest derived predictor. Ad hoc scaling of derived indices is a common
shortcut, and it can move predictors outside their physical range with no visible warning.

## Implications for livestock industries and biosecurity

@tbl-mgmt summarises the management implications by zone. First, the persistent core carries most of
the cattle exposed to *H. longicornis*, and its exposure is unaffected by climate change under any scenario. Theileriosis
control there should be planned as a permanent requirement, with treatment timing adjusted to a lengthening questing season. The indicative cost projections
should be read as an index of change in exposure, not as a forecast. Costs depend on herd immunity and
are concentrated in naive animals, and the estimate we scaled excludes the dairy sector [@shephard2022].
Second, the northern and inland margins are likely to become less suitable, starting now. Investment in
long-term tick-control infrastructure there should account for declining suitability. Because the
process model and the refugia analysis both suggest that losses will be patchy and slower than the SDM implies,
monitoring should come before any reduction in control. Irrigated dairy districts and forested gullies are
where persistence is most likely. Third, climate change will not open new areas. New
incursions will therefore occur in districts that are already suitable but uninfested, and they will
arrive with livestock. The Western District of Victoria and the New England Tablelands combine suitable climate,
large cattle populations and proximity to infested areas, and should be the focus of risk-based
surveillance. Tasmania is climatically suitable throughout and lacks records over most of its area.
Its low modelled introduction risk rests on an assumed sea-crossing penalty, and a precautionary
allocation of surveillance there is prudent. Finally, the people living in suitable climate are the population that would be exposed if
*H. longicornis*-borne zoonotic pathogens, such as the bandaviruses causing severe fever with
thrombocytopenia syndrome in East Asia [@yu2011], were introduced. This supports integrating tick and
pathogen surveillance under a One Health framework.

::: {.primary-table}
::: {#tbl-mgmt}
| Zone | Where | Evidence | Implication |
|---|---|---|---|
| Persistent core | Coastal and highland NSW south of ~30°S; eastern and southern Victoria; Tasmania | Suitable in ≥ 80% of GCMs (`r fmt(mg("245_2041-2060", "Persistent (robust)"), 0)` × 10³ km², SSP2-4.5 2041–2060; `r fmt(mg("370_2081-2100", "Persistent (robust)"), 0)` × 10³ km², SSP3-7.0 2081–2100); most exposed cattle; questing season +`r fmt(ps("245_2041-2060")$dMa_core, 1)` to +`r fmt(ps("370_2081-2100")$dMa_core, 1)` months | Maintain theileriosis control as a permanent requirement; adjust treatment timing to a longer season |

## Limitations

The model describes climatic suitability at about 5 km. It ignores microclimate, vegetation,
irrigation, host density and land use, all of which affect local abundance, so the maps indicate where
populations can persist climatically, not where the tick is present or abundant. Cloglog output is a
relative index, and binary maps depend on the threshold, although projected change was insensitive to
the choice (@supptbl-ensens, @supptbl-thr). Omission under spatial-block cross-validation was above the
nominal 0.10, indicating some residual over-fitting. The target-group data used for bias correction are
themselves uneven. Bisexual and parthenogenetic populations were pooled in the native range. Because only
the parthenogenetic form occurs in Australia, its niche may be better represented by the native
localities it occupies, which a lineage-resolved dataset could test. Future
predictors are delta-downscaled monthly climatologies and represent changes in mean climate, not in
variability or extremes such as heatwaves and droughts, which may matter more for tick survival. The
Hargreaves PET formulation may overstate increases in evaporative demand under warming, making the
moisture-driven losses conservative upper bounds. The projections assume that the niche is conserved
and that populations do not adapt within the projection horizon. They describe equilibrium
suitability, not the rate at which populations change. The extension analyses add further assumptions:
livestock and population are fixed at 2010 and 2020; the gravity model uses distance as a proxy for
livestock movement; the process model uses monthly climatologies and omits diapause and host finding,
and two of its structural choices were made after inspecting a first version; and the surveillance
model treats units as independent and detection as perfectly specific.

## Future work

Three steps would most improve these results. First, replacing the distance-based gravity model with
observed movement networks from the National Livestock Identification System, and adding wildlife
hosts, would sharpen estimates of introduction risk. Second, hindcasting the documented spread of the
tick in Australia during the twentieth century and in the United States since 2017 would test whether
the model predicts change over time as well as pattern in space [@yates2018]. Structured surveys in at-risk and
unrecorded areas would provide true absences. Third, weighting GCMs by regional skill, using regionally
downscaled projections and linking exposure estimates to herd-level theileriosis data would reduce the
largest remaining uncertainties. Reporting the model with the ODMAP protocol [@zurell2020] and publishing the
rasters through an interactive map would make the results easier for agencies to adopt.

## Conclusions

The climatic niche of *H. longicornis* has been conserved during its invasion of Oceania. A model
calibrated across all ranges predicts its Australian distribution well, provided it includes an absolute temperature
gradient and corrects for regional imbalance in sampling. Climate change will contract the Australian
range from its warm and dry margins, by about a tenth already and by a fifth to almost a half by the end
of the century depending on emissions. The core range in south-eastern Australia and Tasmania remains
suitable throughout. Gains are negligible, so new incursions will be driven by livestock movement into
suitable, uninfested districts. Management should maintain theileriosis control across the persistent
core, monitor the warm margin rather than assume retreat, and target surveillance at the Western District of
Victoria, the New England Tablelands and, as a precaution, Tasmania.
